To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Gβγ dimenters are required for the inhibitory action of mGlu6 on TRPM1 channels.
the G-protein–mediating inhibition of the Trpm1 channel requires the Gβ γ dimer, and that the G βγ dimer closes the Trpm1 channels in all cell types tested.
Gβγ is the effector that closes the TRPM channels in bipolar cells and in HEK and HEM cells.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how G proteins control TRPM1 channels, which are important for the function of ON bipolar cells in the visual system.
the role of the transient receptor potential (TRP) family of cation channels in sensory transduction.
the function of a G-protein–mediating inhibition of the TRP channel TRPM1.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Gβγ complex, but not G protein itself, inhibits TRPM channels.
Gβγ is the effector molecule that mediates the inhibition of TRPM1 channels.
TRPM1 is inhibited by Gβγ.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Gβγ complex mediates the inhibitory action of the G-protein–linked metabotropic glutamate receptors on the TRPM1 cation channel.
the G-protein–mediation inhibition of the TRPM1 channels is a critical step for the ON pathway function in the visual system.
G-protein–mediation of the inhibitory effect on TRPM1 requires Gβγ.
The main takeaway from our work is that
TRPM1 is closed by the dissociated Gβγ diter, and this is the mechanism by which the mGlu6 cascade regulates TRPM1.
the Gβγ dimers released from Gαo as a result of mGlu receptor activation are responsible for inhibiting TRPM1 channels and thus for initiating the signal cascade that results in visual responses.
TRPM1 is closed by the Gβγ dimers released upon activation of the mGlu6/Go cascade.
